Learning Objectives
Consider the normal growth and development of the musculoskeletal system.
Describe the structure and function of the zones within the physis.
Identify the location of insults within the physis and the resulting disease states.
Examine the role of hormones in normal and abnormal growth and development.


Formation of the Bony Skeleton
NumberedList1">
Intramembranous bone formation is achieved via the formation of a calcified osteoid
matrix by osteoblasts inside a cartilage framework. This type of bone formation can be
found at the periosteal surfaces of bone and in parts of the pelvis, scapula, clavicles, and
skull.
Endochondral ossification occurs at the growth plates and within fracture callus and is
characterized by osteoblast production of osteoid onto a cartilaginous framework. The
cartilage framework ultimately is resorbed.
Vertebral and Limb Bud Development
4 weeks of gestation
The vertebrate limb begins as an outpouching of the lateral body wall.
Formation of the limb is controlled along three cardinal axes of the limb bud to form an
anlage: from proximal-distal, anterior-posterior, and dorsal-ventral.
Interactions between the ectoderm and mesoderm characterize development along each
axis and are governed by the interaction of fibroblast growth factors, bone morphogenetic
proteins, and several homeobox genes.
6 weeks of gestation
The mesenchymal condensations that represent the limbs and digits chondrify.
The mesenchymal cells differentiate into chondrocytes.
7 weeks of gestation
The chondrocytes hypertrophy, and the local matrix begins to calcify.
A periosteal sleeve of bone forms in a circumferential fashion around the midshaft of each
anlage, and intramembranous bone formation begins to occur via direct ossification.
8 weeks of gestation

Vertebral and Limb Bud Development
Development of the limb bud/extremities and vertebral column happens at a predictable
time and sequence during gestation. In situ or teratogenic insults during each time
period result in an expected limb or vertebral difference.
Formation of Endochondral Bone and Ossification Centers

Formation of Endochondral Bone and Ossification Centers
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:18 PM
AAOS | Growth and Embryology
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001049
3/27

As development continues, the osteoblasts produce an osteoid matrix on the surface of
the calcified cartilaginous bars and form the primary trabeculae of endochondral bone.
The osteoclasts aid in creation of the medullary canal by removing the primary
trabecular bone. This process of formation and absorption enlarges the primary center
of ossification so it becomes the growth region on each end of a newly developing bone.
These growth regions differentiate further and become well-defined growth plates.
Division within the epiphyseal plate is coupled with the deposition of bone at the
metaphyseal side of the bud, and long bone growth begins. At a specific time in the
development of each long bone, a secondary center of ossification develops within the
chondroepiphysis. The secondary center of ossification typically grows in a spherical
fashion and accounts for the centripetal growth of the long bone. The rates of division
within the centers of ossification ultimately determine the overall contour of each joint.
Bone and Joint Biology: Joint Structure and Function
Normal Physis
Structure, Organization, and Function
The function of the physis is related to its structure. In its simplest form, the physis comprises
three histologically distinct zones surrounded by a fibrous component and bounded by a bony
metaphyseal component.
The three cellular zones of the physis are the reserve zone, proliferative zone, and
hypertrophic zone (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Photomicrograph shows the structure and zones of the epiphyseal plate (×220). (Science
Source, New York, NY.)

Structure, Organization, and Function
The reserve zone is adjacent to the secondary center of ossification and is characterized
by a sparse distribution of cells in a vast matrix. Cellular proliferation in this zone is
sporadic, and the chondrocytes in this region do not contribute to longitudinal growth.
Type II collagen content is highest here. Blood is supplied to this zone via the terminal
branches of the epiphyseal artery, which enter the secondary center of ossification.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:18 PM
AAOS | Growth and Embryology
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001049
5/27

The proliferative zone is characterized by longitudinal columns of flattened cells. The
uppermost cell in each column is the progenitor cell, which is responsible for
longitudinal growth. The total longitudinal growth of the physis depends on the number
of cell divisions of the progenitor cell. The rate at which the cells divide is influenced by
mechanical and hormonal factors. The matrix of the proliferative zone comprises a
nonuniform array of collagen fibrils and matrix vesicles. Proliferative zone chondrocytes
also are supplied by the terminal branches of the epiphyseal artery; however, these
vessels do not penetrate the proliferative zone but rather terminate at the uppermost
cell. These vessels deliver the oxygen and nutrients that facilitate the cellular division
and matrix production that occur within this zone.
The cells in the hypertrophic zone are 5 to 10 times the size of those in the proliferative
zone. Because of growth in the columns, this is the weakest layer. Fractures in the physis
occur through this layer. The role of the chondrocytes in the hypertrophic zone is the
synthesis of novel matrix proteins. The hypertrophic zone has the highest content of
glycolytic enzymes, and the chondrocytes participate in matrix mineralization via the
synthesis of alkaline phosphatase, neutral proteases, and type X collagen. The
hypertrophic zone is avascular; fractures can occur through the hypertrophic zone of the
physis.
The metaphysis begins distal to the hypertrophic zone and removes the mineralized
cartilaginous matrix of the hypertrophic zone. The metaphysis also is involved in bone
formation and the histologic remodeling of cancellous trabeculae. The main nutrient
artery of the long bone enters at the mid-diaphysis and then bifurcates and sends a
branch within the medullary canal to each metaphysis. The capillary loops of these
arteries terminate at the bone-cartilage interface of the epiphyseal plate (Figure 2).

The periphery of the physis is surrounded by the groove of Ranvier and the
perichondrial ring of LaCroix. Three cell types are found in the groove of Ranvier: an
osteoblast-type cell, a chondrocyte-type cell, and a fibroblast-type cell. These cells are
active in cell division and contribute to bone formation, latitudinal growth, and
anchorage to the perichondrium. The ring of LaCroix is a fibrous collagenous network
that is continuous with the groove of Ranvier and the metaphysis. It functions as
mechanical support at the bone-cartilage junction.


Biochemistry
The reserve zone has the lowest intracellular and ionized calcium content. Oxygen
tension is low in this zone. Oxygen tension is highest in the proliferative zone, secondary
to its rich vascular supply. Abundant glycogen stores and a high oxygen tension support
aerobic metabolism in the proliferative chondrocyte. Oxygen tension in the hypertrophic
zone is low, secondary to the avascular nature of the region. Because of this low oxygen
tension, energy production in the hypertrophic zone occurs via anaerobic glycolysis of
the glycogen stored in the proliferative zone. In the upper hypertrophic zone, a switch
from adenosine triphosphate production to calcium production occurs. After the
glycogen stores have been depleted, calcium is released. This is the mechanism by which
the matrix is calcified. The region of the hypertrophic zone in which mineralization
occurs is known as the zone of provisional calcification. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
and many other skeletal abnormalities result from a hypertrophic zone abnormality.
Several enzymes are involved in cartilage matrix turnover, including metalloproteinases,
which depend on the presence of calcium and zinc for activity. Collagenase, gelatinase,
and stromelysin are produced by the epiphyseal plate chondrocytes in an inactive form
and then activated by interleukin-1, plasmin, or tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases.
The metaphysis (which is characterized by anaerobic metabolism, vascular stasis, and
low oxygen tension, secondary to the limited blood supply to the region) removes the
mineralized cartilage matrix and the unmineralized last transverse septum of the
hypertrophic zone. The unmineralized portion is removed via lysosomal enzymes, and
the cartilaginous lacunae are invaded by endothelial and perivascular cells.
After the removal process is complete, osteoblasts begin the remodeling process, in
which the osteoblasts progressively lay down bone on the cartilage template, creating an
area of woven bone on a central core that is known as primary trabecular bone. The
primary trabecular bone is resorbed via osteoclastic activity and replaced by lamellar
bone, which represents the secondary bony trabeculae. This remodeling process occurs
around the periphery and subperiosteal regions of the metaphysis and results in
funnelization, a narrowing of the diameter of the metaphysis to meet the diaphysis.

Pathophysiology
Overview
Most physeal abnormalities can be attributed to a defect within a specific zone or to a
particular malfunction in the system.
Most physeal abnormalities affect the reserve zone; however, no currently available evidence
suggests that any disease state originates from cytopathology unique to the reserve zone.
Any disease state that affects the matrix will have an effect on the proliferative zone.
Achondroplasia

Achondroplasia
Achondroplasia originates in the chondrocytes of the proliferative zone. The disorder
usually results from a single amino acid substitution, which causes a defect in fibroblast
growth factor receptor 3 (Table 2; Figure 3).


Jansen Metaphyseal Chondrodysplasia
A mutation in the parathyroid hormone–related protein (PTHrP) receptor affects the
negative feedback loop in which PTHrP slows the conversion of proliferating
chondrocytes to hypertrophic chondrocytes. The mutation in the receptor results in a
continuously active state that is the molecular basis for Jansen metaphyseal
chondrodysplasia. Because this receptor is the shared receptor for parathyroid hormone
(PTH), hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia may occur.
Physeal Mineralization

Physeal Mineralization
Physeal mineralization is a unique process because of the specialized blood supply to
the epiphyseal plate, its unique energy metabolism, and its handling of intracellular
calcium stores. The major factors that affect physis mineralization are intracellular
calcium homeostasis, the extracellular matrix vesicles, and the extracellular
macromolecules. Various microenvironmental factors and systemic hormones also
modulate this process.
The role of intracellular calcium in matrix mineralization is so important that the
mitochondria in the chondrocytes are specialized for calcium transport. Compared with
non-mineralizing cells, the chondrocyte mitochondria have a greater capacity for calcium
accumulation and can store calcium in a labile form so it can be used for release.
Histologic studies have demonstrated that mitochondrial calcium accumulates in the
upper two-thirds of the hypertrophic zone and is depleted in the lower chondrocytes. If
the mitochondrial calcium is released in the lower cells, matrix mineralization occurs
(Figure 4).
The initial site for matrix calcification is unclear; however, data exist to support the role
of the matrix vesicle in this process. The matrix vesicles are rich in alkaline phosphatase
and neutral proteases, which are critical in promoting mineralization.

Effects of Hormones and Growth Factors on the Epiphyseal Plate
Influence on Physeal Mechanics
Hormones, growth factors, and vitamins have been shown to influence the physis via
mechanisms such as chondrocyte proliferation and maturation, macromolecule synthesis,
intracellular calcium homeostasis, and matrix mineralization.


Influence on Physeal Mechanics
Each physeal zone may be targeted by one or more factors that help to mediate the
cytologic characteristics unique to that zone. These factors may be exogenous or
endogenous to the epiphyseal plate. Paracrine factors are produced by cells within the
physis and act within the physis but then on another cell type. Autocrine factors act on
the cells that produced them.
The thyroid hormones thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) act on the proliferative
and upper hypertrophic zone chondrocytes via a systemic endocrine effect. T4 is
essential for cartilage growth. It increases DNA synthesis in the cells of the proliferative
zone and affects cell maturation by increasing glycosaminoglycan synthesis, collagen
synthesis, and alkaline phosphatase activity. Excess T4 results in protein catabolism; a
deficiency of T4 results in growth retardation, cretinism, and abnormal degradation of
mucopolysaccharides.
PTH also acts on the proliferative and upper hypertrophic zone chondrocytes. PTH has a
direct mitogenic effect on epiphyseal chondrocytes. In addition, PTH stimulates
proteoglycan synthesis via an increase in intracellular ionized calcium and the
stimulation of protein kinase C. PTHrP is a cytokine with autocrine or paracrine action.
The common PTHrP-PTH receptor has a role in the conversion of the small cell
chondrocyte to the hypertrophic phenotype.
Calcitonin is a peptide hormone that is produced by the parafollicular cells of the
thyroid. It acts primarily in the lower hypertrophic zone to accelerate epiphyseal plate
calcification and cell maturation.
Adrenal corticoids, or glucocorticoids, are steroid hormones primarily produced by the
adrenal cortex. These hormones primarily affect the zones of cellular differentiation and

9/3/26, 4:18 PM

15/27

proliferation. The primary influence of the glucocorticoids is a decrease in proliferation
of the chondroprogenitor cells in the zone of differentiation. Supraphysiologic amounts
of these hormones result in growth retardation via a depression of glycolysis and a
reduction of energy stores.
The primary active androgen metabolite is postulated to be dihydrotestosterone, based
on the presence of this receptor in male and female epiphyseal plate tissue. The role of
the androgens is to regulate mineralization in the lower part of the epiphyseal plate,
increase the deposition of glycogen and lipids in cells, and increase the number of
proteoglycans in the cartilage matrix.
Growth hormone is produced by the pituitary gland and is essential for physis function.
The effects of growth hormone are mediated by the somatomedins, a group of peptide
factors. If growth hormone binds to epiphyseal chondrocytes, insulin-like growth factor 1
(IGF-1) is released locally. Therefore, growth hormone regulates not only the number of
cells containing the insulin-like growth factor receptor but also the synthesis of insulin-
like growth factor 1 in all zones of the physis.
The active metabolites of vitamin D are the 1,25- and 24,25-dihydroxylated forms, both
of which are produced by the liver and kidneys. A direct mitogenic effect has been
reported with 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. The metabolite substantially increases DNA
synthesis and inhibits proteoglycan synthesis. The level of vitamin D metabolites is
highest in the proliferative zone; no metabolites are found in the hypertrophic zone.
Vitamin A (carotenoids) is essential for the metabolism of epiphyseal cartilage. A
deficiency of vitamin A results in impairment of cell maturation, which ultimately causes
abnormal bone shape. Excessive vitamin A leads to bone weakness secondary to
increases in lysosomal body membrane fragility.
Vitamin C is a cofactor in the enzymatic synthesis of collagen; therefore, it is necessary
for the development of the physis.

Physeal Injury

Physeal Injury
The weakest structure in the ends of the long bones is the physis, and the weakest
region within the physis itself is the hypertrophic zone. Although the perichondral ring
provides some stability, shear forces frequently are high and may lead to fractures at the
end of a long lever arm (thin, long extremities). Physeal injuries occur if the mechanical
demands exceed the mechanical strength of the epiphysis-to-growth plate metaphyseal
complex. The mechanical properties of the physis are described by the Hueter-Volkmann
law, which states that increasing compression across the physis leads to decreasing
growth (Figure 5).

Physeal Properties

Physeal Properties
The morphology of the physis allows it to adapt its form to follow the contours of
principal tensile stresses. The contours allow the physis to be subjected to compressive
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:18 PM
AAOS | Growth and Embryology
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001049
18/27

stress. The tensile properties of the physis have been determined by controlled uniaxial
tension tests in the bovine femur. The ultimate strain at failure has been shown to be
uniform throughout the epiphyseal plate. The anterior and inferior regions of the physis
are the strongest. Mechanical forces can influence the shape and length of the growing
bone, and studies have demonstrated that mechanical forces are present and may
influence bone development during the earliest stages of endochondral ossification. The
biologic interface between the metaphyseal ossification front and the adjacent
proliferative cartilage is partially determined by mechanical forces, initially in the form of
muscle contractions. The function of the physis and its mechanical properties appear to
be influenced by the internal structure and external mechanical factors.

Pathologic States Affecting Growth
All cartilage matrix defects produce some form of skeletal dysplasia, with varied degrees
of effect on articular and physeal cartilage. Abnormalities of type II collagen cause Kniest
dysplasia and some types of Stickler syndrome and spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia.
Abnormalities of type IX collagen cause some forms of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia.
Defects in type X collagen cause the Schmid-type metaphyseal chondrodysplasia.
Diastrophic dysplasia is a classic example of a defect in proteoglycan metabolism. The
disorder is caused by a mutation in the sulfate transporter molecule, which results in
under-sulfation of the proteoglycan matrix. The phenotype is short stature and
characteristic severe equinovarus feet.
Mucopolysaccharidoses are six disorders that result from defects in the proteoglycan
metabolism (Table 3). These disorders are caused by a defect in the enzymes involved in
proteoglycan metabolism with a resultant accumulation of undegraded
glycosaminoglycans (Table 4). The clinical presentation of each mucopolysaccharidosis
depends on the specific enzyme defect and the resultant glycoprotein accumulation.
Common to all six disease states is a toxic effect on the central nervous system, the
skeleton, or the ocular or visceral system.
Hypophosphatasia is an autosomal recessive defect in alkaline phosphatase
(characteristic laboratory finding) with resultant normal serum levels of calcium and
phosphate but an inability of the matrix to calcify. The hypertrophic zone widens, but no
mineralization occurs in the osteoid that is laid down. The zone of provisional
calcification never forms. The histologic appearance and effect are similar to nutritional
rickets, with a resultant inhibition of growth. Hypophosphatemic familial rickets is a sex-
linked dominant disorder characterized by low serum calcium and phosphorus levels.
Alkaline phosphatase activity is high, with resultant abnormal conversion of vitamin D to
its metabolites. The skeletal changes observed are those typical of nutritional rickets.
Bacterial infection typically affects the metaphyseal portion of the physis. This is because
of the slow circulation, low oxygen tension, and deficiency of the reticuloendothelial

system in this area. Bacteria become lodged in the vascular sinusoids, resulting in the
production of small abscesses in the area. If the infection extends into the Haversian
canals, osteomyelitis of the cortical bone ensues, with associated subperiosteal abscess.
In the first year of life, cartilage canals may persist across growth plates and serve as an
additional conduit for the spread of infection. Severe infection may cause local or total
cessation of growth; in most instances, inhibited or angular growth results.
Depending on the dose, irradiation may result in shortened bones with increased width
because of the preferential negative effect on longitudinal chondroblastic proliferation,
with sparing of latitudinal bone growth.
Nutritional rickets results from the abnormal processing of calcium, phosphorus, and
vitamin D. The common result is failure to mineralize the matrix in the zone of
provisional calcification. The hypertrophic zone is expanded greatly, with widening of the
physis and flaring of the metaphysis observed on plain radiographs (Figure 6).
Caused by vitamin C deficiency, scurvy results in a decrease in chondroitin sulfate and
collagen synthesis. The greatest deficiency in collagen synthesis is seen in the
metaphysis, where the demand for type I collagen is highest during new bone formation.
Characteristic radiographic findings of scurvy are the Frankel line (a transverse dense
white line that represents the zone of provisional calcification), metaphyseal flaring, and
osteopenia of the metaphysis. Clinical findings include microfractures, hemorrhages,
and collapse of the metaphysis.
